inputs: Authorized inbound traffic sources, accurate ads and landing pages, versioned recipient-specific disclosures, TrustedForm or Jornaya evidence where applicable, suppression records and permitted recording notices.

Ringba or Retreaver configuration, documented buyer ping-post endpoints, buyer authorization or licensing checks, vertical-specific eligibility rules, capacities and payout terms including any 90–120-second duration threshold.
Traffic cost data, call-detail records, transfer and consent events, buyer acceptance receipts, duplicate identifiers, dispute reason codes and restricted-access retention settings.
operator_plays.mechanism: Use Ringba or Retreaver-supported routing and buyer integrations to auction qualified inbound calls through sub-second ping-post trees, earning the spread between accepted buyer payouts and traffic acquisition costs. Operate separate programs for ACA/Medicare, auto/home insurance, mass-tort legal intake and emergency home services, with recipient-specific consent where required, sector-specific transfer restrictions and privacy-minimized bid payloads. TrustedForm or Jornaya records can support evidence of the actual named-recipient disclosure but do not independently establish valid consent; negotiated 90–120-second duration triggers qualify payment only alongside genuine caller intent, buyer acceptance and applicable contract terms.
metrics: Net contribution per qualified call: collected buyer revenue minus acquisition, telephony, routing, verification and refund costs.
Routing quality: p95 auction latency, accepted-connection rate, abandonment rate and buyer capacity rejection rate by vertical.
Evidence and dispute quality: percentage of transfers with required recipient-specific permission records, duplicate rate, complaint rate and payout reversal rate.
operator_plays.name: Consent-Verified Inbound RTB Pay-Per-Call Exchange Operator

platform_risks.detection_metric: Consent-recipient mismatch count, complaint and reversal rates by source, and anomalous clustering of call endings immediately after the billing threshold.
platform_risks.failure_mode: A buyer or routing platform rejects calls or suspends the program because consent, marketing representations or traffic quality fails applicable requirements.
platform_risks.fallback: Stop affected sources and transfers, preserve evidence securely, refund invalid billings and resume only with corrected disclosures, permitted compensation structures and verified buyer acceptance.
platform_risks.impact: Payout reversals, account suspension, consumer complaints and potential regulatory or contractual exposure.
platform_risks.trigger: Recipient mismatches, misleading ACA/Medicare advertising, restricted legal-referral fee structures, excessive duplicates or calls padded to cross a duration threshold.

workflow: 1. Approve legitimate traffic sources and buyer contracts, segregate verticals, and establish how each caller receives accurate recipient disclosures without misleading benefit claims or prohibited steering.

2. Screen intent, geography, duplicates and applicable transfer restrictions; obtain required permission before transmitting personal information and send only permitted minimal qualification metadata in bid requests.

3. Run the supported sub-second auction with timeouts and capacity checks, identify the selected recipient and obtain any required recipient-specific permission before transfer, then connect the caller without artificially extending duration.
4. Reconcile buyer acceptance and any 90–120-second billing condition against call records, resolve disputes, suppress invalid sources and settle only genuine, contract-qualified calls.

chapters.question_prompt: What is pay-per-call, how does the money flow between publishers, networks and buyers, and how should a beginner pick a lane and a niche?
chapters.title: Pay-Per-Call Fundamentals: The Model, the Vocabulary, and Choosing Your Lane
chapters.subtitle: Inbound vs. outbound calls, core PPC terminology, pay-per-call vs. pay-per-lead, affiliate vs. local client lead gen, SEO and rank-and-rent call sites, niche selection, startup requirements, and the industry's biggest obstacles
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from Ringba, TrackDrive, Matt Wacek, John Ventura, ceohec, John Casto, Leadbase and WordsAtScale converge on one model: a buyer pays a fixed price for a live inbound call that clears pre-agreed rules on duration, geography and hours, and the publisher or broker pockets the spread between what traffic costs and what the call sells for. The street numbers are concrete: TrackDrive's $50 revenue, $35 payout, $15 margin split; ceohec's 40% minimum markup that turns a $150 roofing call into $210; Ringba's $25 call costing $2 to generate; Ventura's $150-$400 personal-injury and $70-$1,000 water-damage payouts. The fight is over the starting lane: Leadbase argues pay-per-lead is two and a half times likelier to succeed for beginners, Wacek weighs easy network approval against fatter direct-client checks, and Casto would rather sell 100 calls than 1,000 leads.

key_metrics.label: Network Margin Per Qualified Call
key_metrics.value: $15 per call ($50 revenue minus $35 publisher payout)
key_metrics.context: Worked example of how revenue, payout and margin split on one call; in a direct buyer-seller deal there is no margin to split.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Pay-per-call is a performance deal in which a business pays only for a live inbound phone call. Ringba frames it as a risk transfer: acquisition risk moves off the advertiser and onto the network or the affiliates promoting the offer, so the buyer can predict cost per customer, and a $10 call closing at 25% lands a customer at roughly $40 every time [4kaOQgGnpJo @ 00:01:48]. TrackDrive's masterclass states the trigger plainly: the advertiser pays because a real consumer had a conversation with the business, and that call must clear rules fixed in advance, usually a minimum length, a specific location and the hours someone is there to answer [_h1_mcKPGjY @ 00:01:28]. The premium rests on intent. A click can be curiosity or an accident, while a call means someone stopped what they were doing to talk to a person. Start & Grow Your Business gives the common floor condition: the caller stays on the line a minute or two so the buyer knows nobody was tricked into dialing, and such calls can pay around $20 each [8qGNYXEyrqI @ 00:01:24]. Matt Wacek strips it to the bone: the marketer bridges the gap between a homeowner with a flooded basement and the water damage contractor equipped to fix it [t7-UhvFv7r4 @ 00:00:15].

Speakers agree on the cast. TrackDrive lists the consumer, the publisher (also called an affiliate or seller) who creates the reason to call, the advertiser or buyer who answers, and an optional network that tracks, routes, bills the buyer, pays the publisher and keeps the difference [_h1_mcKPGjY @ 00:06:39]. Its vocabulary episode puts numbers on the split: a buyer pays $50 revenue, the publisher earns a $35 payout, and the $15 gap is margin; in a direct deal there is no margin to split, and a cap, concurrency limit or billable duration can kill a call's earnings no matter how good the traffic was [V1FTIO7peWA @ 00:04:15]. ceohec runs the same chain as a broker play: one party is the media buyer generating calls who does not know how to acquire buyers, the broker in the middle connects them and, in that speaker's words, makes all the money, and the buyer is the roofer, insurance agent or lawyer who sells [Rcc1hu6P28g @ 00:00:30]. Ringba warns that the middle is not a straight pipe: depending on caller information, concurrency, hours and capacity, the same network may route your calls to many different buyers, load balancing them all over the place [4kaOQgGnpJo @ 00:11:21]. Everyone gets paid only when the agreed rules are met.

The baseline prerequisites repeat across channels. Ringba's first rule for anyone building a real business is to run their own call tracking, because without it an affiliate cannot verify network statistics, cannot tell if a call was legitimate or even happened, and leaves partners free to steal from them [4kaOQgGnpJo @ 00:07:37]. Adam Young, who co-founded Ringba, says the industry is an incredible opportunity but never easy, and lists the skills that matter: digital marketing to make the phone ring, plus business development, because in pay-per-call you are selling consumers and have to pound the pavement in Skype, Telegram, Facebook and LinkedIn groups and at trade shows [J58YYa45MF4 @ 00:05:24]. Matt Wacek wants the paperwork done before the first offer: a parent company, an EIN, and a W-9 on file, since networks ask for it so they can issue a 1099 and expense the commissions paid [m-08JHhJeok @ 00:05:02]. John Casto adds the operating prerequisite that keeps a campaign alive past its shelf life: a disposition feedback loop, with some buyers sending dispositions daily and others weekly, which let Casto's team scale one solar client to roughly $10 million in revenue since 2016 [XQvPekJ-K8M @ 00:00:24].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The network-affiliate route runs on borrowed numbers. Ringba walks a debt consolidation offer paying $30 per call for callers carrying more than $10,000 in unsecured card debt: get approved, take the network's tracking number, route your own tracking number into theirs, put yours on a mobile ad, and collect when the buyer qualifies the caller [4kaOQgGnpJo @ 00:13:58]. Calls that fail the rules, such as Massachusetts callers sent to an insurance buyer licensed only in California, simply go unpaid. The same speaker recommends separate numbers for each site and marketing channel so you can see which placements work. Getting approved is light. Matt Wacek says networks mainly want a registered business, a look at your creatives, whether a website, videos, Craigslist listings or call-only ads, and a quick phone conversation, after which you can apply to campaigns and potentially run traffic the same day [uxYMcIUwpLA @ 00:00:27]. In Wacek's longer build guide, the cheapest proof is three to five YouTube livestream videos on page one for low-competition city-plus-service terms, each taking under ten minutes, which is generally what it takes for approval [m-08JHhJeok @ 00:09:06]. Before building city pages, Wacek cross-checks the network's zip code spreadsheet, because not every city or state is approved for every offer [m-08JHhJeok @ 00:14:41].

The broker lane is spread trading. ceohec's worked example buys a roofing call from a publisher at $150 on a 120-second buffer, marks it up a 40% minimum to $210, and closes a roofer on a minimum of 10 calls, collecting $2,100 up front while the publisher invoices only $1,500 on net-three to net-ten terms at the end of the week, leaving $600 gross and roughly $450 after a $150 cost to acquire that buyer [Rcc1hu6P28g @ 00:06:32]. The plumbing is a ping: the publisher's routing system asks the broker's platform whether a funded buyer is online, sends the call only when one is, and the buyer's prepaid wallet is debited $210 once the call crosses the buffer [Rcc1hu6P28g @ 00:08:11]. TrackDrive's vocabulary governs the rest of the deal: a cap is the most calls a buyer accepts per hour, day or month, like a law office that handles 35 a day, while concurrency is how many it can take at once, so five agents means the sixth caller waits or goes elsewhere [V1FTIO7peWA @ 00:03:10]. Global Call Forwarding lists the inbound stack behind all of this: IVR, call flow builders, forwarding, routing and call tracking [PWSdRBsFa5Y @ 00:04:09].

Payout benchmarks vary by an order of magnitude, which is why niche selection drives everything. John Ventura quotes $150 to $400 per qualified personal injury call and $200 to $600 or more for active mass tort campaigns, $70 to $1,000 in water damage, $50 to $70 for debt relief plus $150 to $250 enrollment bonuses, and $20 to $40 for auto against $30 to $100 or more for Medicare and health [KAXRt_1Gm_4 @ 00:06:09]. Matt Wacek's floor-to-ceiling range runs from $8 to $12 on low-ticket services up to $400 to $800 per qualified call in addiction recovery, where a center earns $30,000 to $40,000 per customer [t7-UhvFv7r4 @ 00:03:08]. The same speaker pins water damage at $50 to $100 per call through a network while metro clicks cost $200 to $450, arguing a direct client could pay $250 to $500 per qualified lead [uxYMcIUwpLA @ 00:05:07]. WordsAtScale shows how much the receiving category matters by pulling eLocal's public rate card: biohazard cleanup at a $125 to $265 top bid against $10 to $35 for junk removal and cleanouts, so the category you send the call into decides what you earn, and you should search for the category a buyer already pays for rather than your exact niche [DJFaYJ3O7aU @ 00:01:22].

callout.title: Spread, Placement and Funnel Edges Operators Actually Use
callout.body: Small moves that operators credit with widening margins, finding cheap call sources, or squeezing extra calls out of traffic already paid for.
items: Hide the spread: once a campaign works, never let the buyer see your margin; a call sold at $25 might cost $2 to generate and the rest is ongoing profit [Ringba — 4kaOQgGnpJo @ 00:03:16]

Zip-tie test: a movers company hung signs every 100 feet on chain-link fences in front of apartment complexes, each placement on a different tracked number, to see which spots produced moving calls [Adam Young — J58YYa45MF4 @ 00:04:31]
Hybrid funnel: drive urgency on the lead form thank-you page; some Leadbase Pro members get a 40% call rate there, selling the lead and then the call [Leadbase — ewNftdwX784 @ 00:12:52]

Grey-hat Google My Business listing: register the site's brand name at a home address, hide the address and show only a service area for a free call source, which may or may not break Google's terms [Matt Wacek — m-08JHhJeok @ 00:14:55]

sop_steps.title: Pick the Paying Category, Then Pull the Rate Card
sop_steps.action: Choose a niche, map it to the broader category buyers already pay for, and pull the rate card for your city before building anything.
sop_steps.detail: Search your niche plus pay per call and buy your niche calls, check Offervault, and treat the published rate card as a best-case top bid rather than your price [WordsAtScale — DJFaYJ3O7aU @ 00:05:27]

sop_steps.title: Stand Up the Entity and Approval Assets
sop_steps.action: Register the parent company, get an EIN and W-9 ready, and publish three to five page-one livestream videos or a clean site with service-area pages.
sop_steps.detail: Wacek reports three to five first-page YouTube videos are generally what it takes for a network to approve you, and advises avoiding superlatives like the best on approval assets [Matt Wacek — m-08JHhJeok @ 00:09:06]

sop_steps.title: Layer Your Own Tracking Over the Network's Number
sop_steps.action: Buy your own tracking numbers, one per site or channel, and forward them into the network's assigned tracking number.
sop_steps.detail: Ringba routes the affiliate's own tracking number into the network's number on a $30 debt consolidation offer so every call can be audited independently [Ringba — 4kaOQgGnpJo @ 00:13:58]

sop_steps.title: Lock the Qualification Terms in Writing
sop_steps.action: Define minimum call length, service area, hours and duplicate rules, and bill weekly or collect up front for a block of calls.
sop_steps.detail: Put qualified in writing: minimum call length, inside the service area, and not the same caller twice in 30 days, because most fights are about what counts [WordsAtScale — DJFaYJ3O7aU @ 00:05:10]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether a newcomer should sell calls at all. Leadbase runs a business that is 100% pay-per-lead and argues a beginner's success rate in pay-per-call is multiple times lower, because calls demand more investment and creative urgent enough to make someone stop scrolling and dial right now [ewNftdwX784 @ 00:01:50]. Their profitability math sets a $20 insurance or mortgage form lead resold at $40 to $45 against a call costing $50 or more, with a starting risk multiplier closer to five times and a $100 call for someone still learning [ewNftdwX784 @ 00:09:14]. On John Casto's channel the pitch runs the other way: they would rather sell 100 calls than 1,000 leads, because a quality call should net more, scale better, get paused less, and earn higher caps [b2k9lFS6EWI @ 00:02:16]. The same conversation frames getting a Facebook scroller onto the phone as the hardest and most expensive step in the funnel, which is exactly why the affiliate who owns that step holds more power [b2k9lFS6EWI @ 00:01:44]. TrackDrive refuses to crown either model, saying clicks, leads, and calls each win depending on the product, though calls are often the highest-value action [_h1_mcKPGjY @ 00:03:35]. Leadbase's compromise is a ladder: leads first, then appointments, live transfers, and calls [ewNftdwX784 @ 00:14:33].

The second fault line is who stands between you and the business answering the phone. Matt Wacek describes the affiliate-network lane as low friction: apply with a registered business, show your creatives, take one call with an affiliate manager, and you can start running traffic the same day [uxYMcIUwpLA @ 00:00:27]. The price of that comfort is margin. In Wacek's water-damage example a network pays $50 to $100 per qualified call, while the same lead could command $250 to $500 sold direct to a contractor whose clicks cost $200 to $450 [uxYMcIUwpLA @ 00:05:07], and in his whiteboard breakdown a $50 commission usually means the network bills the business about $100 [t7-UhvFv7r4 @ 00:03:53]. WordsAtScale refuses to choose: a marketplace pays less but needs no outreach and has a buyer from day one, while a direct deal pays more and lets you own the relationship, so the marketplace proves your calls are worth something and catches overflow [DJFaYJ3O7aU @ 00:04:22]. TrackDrive adds the structural catch for going direct: there is no margin to split, but no network handles billing either, so each side tracks the numbers, invoices, and pays the other itself [_h1_mcKPGjY @ 00:07:13]. Every version trades convenience against money per call.

Niche advice diverges sharply depending on who is selling it. John Ventura ranks legal first, quoting $150 to $400 per qualified personal-injury call and $200 to $600 or more for active mass-tort campaigns such as Roundup, Camp Lejeune, and PFAS [KAXRt_1Gm_4 @ 00:01:00]. ceohec agrees motor-vehicle-accident work is lucrative, recalling law firms wiring around 30 grand on a test batch, yet calls it a hard niche and steers students toward final expense, ACA, and auto insurance as the easiest entry points [Rcc1hu6P28g @ 00:02:20]. Home services draws the loudest split. Ventura pitches water-damage restoration at $70 to $1,000 per qualified call with an 85% booking rate on exclusive calls [KAXRt_1Gm_4 @ 00:03:28], while Leonidas at PPCBasic tells a beginner flatly that home services is extremely competitive in the US and that auto insurance is the simpler starting lane [mpyPMRohxDQ @ 00:00:43]. Matt Wacek declines to rank at all, insisting every niche is profitable even when big-city plumbing or water-damage clicks cost more than the commission; his workaround is ranking organic pages across thousands of smaller cities instead of buying those clicks [m-08JHhJeok @ 00:05:58]. Payout size and entry difficulty come from different operators running different traffic engines.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest trap is running another company's numbers blind. Ringba says that without your own call tracking you cannot tell whether network statistics are accurate, whether a call was legitimate, or whether it happened at all, which means partners can steal from you plain and simple [4kaOQgGnpJo @ 00:08:13]. Networks running home-built proprietary trackers get extra suspicion because nobody can audit the code, so your own tracking number has to sit in front of theirs [4kaOQgGnpJo @ 00:10:31]. Adam Young frames the same failure from both sides of the trade: operators not tracking calls and return on investment are likely just going to lose a lot of money, the equivalent of flying an airplane blind [J58YYa45MF4 @ 00:08:46]. The second silent killer is the qualification rulebook. TrackDrive sets the billable-duration example at a 60-second minimum where a 40-second caller pays nothing, and warns that a call arriving after a cap fills or when the buyer has no free line may go unpaid no matter how good the traffic was [V1FTIO7peWA @ 00:04:35]. Ringba shows the IVR version: a debt caller pressing one for under $10,000 in unsecured debt, or Massachusetts calls sent to a California-only insurance buyer, probably earns nothing [4kaOQgGnpJo @ 00:12:50].

Getting paid is its own minefield. Leadbase recalls a debt campaign about seven years ago, sold per lead, where the buyer agreed to pay for three of ten sent, turning a $50 cost per lead into $150, and expects the same pattern plus common call-quality disputes in pay-per-call [ewNftdwX784 @ 00:06:55]. They also flag the affiliate-offer illusion: a solar offer paying $30 to $40 a call looks easy until real costs land at $150 to $250 per call and not every call gets paid [ewNftdwX784 @ 00:07:55]. WordsAtScale lists the fine print that burns people: minimum call lengths of roughly 60 to 120 seconds, buyer hours that leave a Sunday-night call unpaid, a seven-day hold before approval, rate cards that move, and a network that owns the buyer instead of you [DJFaYJ3O7aU @ 00:02:20]. Their scam screen is blunt: one network bidding over $900 for biohazard calls had a domain registered that February, no team, no reviews, and WhatsApp contact, which is bait rather than a better buyer [DJFaYJ3O7aU @ 00:03:12]. Direct deals carry a different risk. Matt Wacek says networks rarely skip a bill, but businesses sometimes stiff you, and per-lead terms mean fronting operating cash, with June calls potentially unpaid until mid-July [uxYMcIUwpLA @ 00:08:06]. His leverage: shut off the ads and the faucet of customers closes [uxYMcIUwpLA @ 00:07:02].

Volume also carries legal and reputational exposure. John Casto says the TCPA demands attention, recalls running a call center on a Duke Energy contract where the client expected complaints as proof of volume, and warns that once a litigator sues your client, you are on the hook too [XQvPekJ-K8M @ 00:03:23]. Casto adds that misleading solar ads built on Tesla get clicks but get you shut off by the client and marked in a small industry, admitting their own operation paid what it owed after past compliance issues [XQvPekJ-K8M @ 00:04:41]. Leonidas reports auto-insurance operators running fake AI videos on Facebook to push people into calling, and calls SMS a big but really dangerous channel in the US [mpyPMRohxDQ @ 00:01:31]. The economics check is plain arithmetic. Ringba's buyer math: $10 a call at a 25% close ratio means roughly $40 to acquire each customer [4kaOQgGnpJo @ 00:01:48]. ceohec's broker math: buy a roofing call at $150 on a 120-second buffer, mark it up 40% to $210, sell a ten-call block, and keep $600 gross, closer to $450 after the roughly $150 spent acquiring that buyer [Rcc1hu6P28g @ 00:06:49]. Run both sides of that equation before routing a single call at scale.

callout.title: Four Checks Before a Single Call Routes at Scale
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, dispute, or near-miss the operators reported. Clear all four before you scale spend.

chapters.question_prompt: How do I set up a call tracking platform and plug into real-time bidding and call exchanges as a seller or buyer?
chapters.title: Platform Setup and Real-Time Bidding for Calls
chapters.subtitle: Ringba account, campaign and target setup, trackable numbers, seller ring trees and RingbaX buyer campaigns, dynamic ring tree targets, programmatic RTB mechanics, overflow routing, and Retreaver and TrackDrive campaign setup
chapters.executive_summary: Ringba, TrackDrive, ExclusiveLiveCall, ceohec, and Decoding Ads all describe call RTB as ping-post for live phone calls. The platform pings buyers with call data, bids and durations come back in a couple hundred milliseconds, and the call routes to the best expected payout before the phone rings. The consensus prerequisites are unique tracking numbers per publisher, owning your own numbers, eligibility filters on geo, hours, caps, and concurrency, and failover so an unanswered winner never kills a paid call. The street mechanics include Ringba ring trees with a $29.01 minimum-revenue floor over static fallbacks, and RingbaX's 10-second dial and 3,000 ms ping timeouts. They also include ceohec's Retreaver build at about 4 cents a minute, with TTL 45, a 5-second timeout, and an 8-second billing buffer. Practitioners split on static versus RTB buyers, Ringba versus Retreaver, and highest-bid versus earnings-per-call routing.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner here treats real-time bidding as the ping-post model ported from lead gen to live calls. Ringba frames it plainly. The caller dials, and the platform pings every programmatic buyer with mapped metadata such as geography and call category. Buyers return a bid, a required duration, and sometimes a dynamic destination number. The call is then routed before the phone even rings, all inside a couple hundred milliseconds [yat7hRHHsKY @ 00:01:10]. ceohec, operating on Retreaver, uses the same vocabulary from the street side. Static means no ping post. RTB means the buyer's system is pinged to see if a buyer is available, and then the call is posted through. In ceohec's view, most operators getting into pay per call run RTB unless they have one buyer who can absorb volume [RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:04:42]. TrackDrive lists ping post as a fifth routing mode alongside priority, weight, highest bid, and earnings per call. It describes the ping as a quick message asking whether the buyer wants the call and what they will pay [9uZila67hss @ 00:02:52]. ExclusiveLiveCall adds the coverage angle. With a ping integration you do not need the downstream buyer's destination number loaded into your platform, because the external network or marketplace returns both the bid and the routing instructions in real time [Hnh5huLjUoE @ 00:06:45].

The second point of agreement is that attribution gets set before any money moves. TrackDrive's rule is one tracking number per publisher and campaign, because two publishers sharing a number kills the ability to say who earned the call and breeds disputes. A sub ID scheme on top tells you which ad, page, or placement produced the call, which TrackDrive calls gold for diagnosing source performance [9uZila67hss @ 00:03:29]. ExclusiveLiveCall pushes the same logic down to the traffic source. It splits one roofing site across separate numbers for Google Ads, SEO, and each subpublisher, so origin follows the call through every routing decision [Hnh5huLjUoE @ 00:01:07]. Decoding Ads runs programmatic SEO sites with many numbers on the page. They advise against dropping a pay-per-call network's number directly onto the site. Instead, use your own number and route it yourself through Ringba, which also lets you stand up your own network by adding publishers [OFst3KoUCj0 @ 00:00:38]. Ringba's onboarding shows how cheap that first number is to get. It offers on-demand toll-free and local DID inventory in over 60 countries. The number is auto-assigned to you until publishers exist, and the campaign name carries through every report [8ojiGzzsrV0 @ 00:01:17].

Third, nobody lets a paid-for call die at a busy signal. Ringba's position is that if the winning ping buyer does not answer, drops, or returns busy, the platform reruns the process. It then routes to another ping buyer or a normal static buyer, so the ping tree inherits every standard routing rule [yat7hRHHsKY @ 00:04:41]. Ringba's Jordan Soto gives the buyer-side reason the model pays. Buyers can deny calls when the floor has no capacity or the caller is a bad fit, and they can bid harder on high-intent callers or when seats are empty. Soto says this yields higher payouts, fewer abandoned calls, and fatter margins [VTCVhKxmT1o @ 00:00:20]. ExclusiveLiveCall walks the eligibility funnel call by call. Start with ten buyers on a campaign. Strip out the one not covering the zip, the closed one, the one capped for the day, the one at max concurrency, and the one rejecting the traffic source, and maybe three remain [Hnh5huLjUoE @ 00:04:00]. Overflow then tries buyer B and C, because the publisher may already have paid Google $50 to $100 for that click [Hnh5huLjUoE @ 00:10:01]. TrackDrive keeps the two jobs separate when diagnosing problems. A call that went to the wrong place is a routing failure, and a call that should have been stopped is a filter failure [9uZila67hss @ 00:04:10].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Inside Ringba the build order is campaign, number, target, then payout. The account walkthrough starts with verifying billing documents, or service gets disrupted. A wizard then names the campaign, picks the country, issues a toll-free or local DID, and creates the first target. Use SIP whenever the target accepts it, because it connects faster, sounds better, and converts better. Phone-number targets must include the country code [8ojiGzzsrV0 @ 00:02:20]. The campaign training layers on the controls that protect margin. These include reporting duplicate calls, treating anonymous callers as duplicates, and paying out once per caller regardless of publisher. Recording is on by default, with an option to trim silence. Payouts can be fixed amounts triggered on call length, connection, inbound call, or conversion, or a revenue share with limits [BOFMLupLrSM @ 00:01:12]. On each target, the connection timeout defaults to 30 seconds before the call reroutes, and priority 1 is the highest. Two targets with equal weight split traffic 50/50. Caps run on conversions, connections, or revenue at overall, monthly, daily, or hourly levels, with a separate concurrency ceiling [BOFMLupLrSM @ 00:06:12]. The targets training adds tag routing filters with AND and OR rules. It also adds an RPC setting that controls how estimated revenue per call is calculated for each destination [2p-PtocR9pE @ 00:02:29].

Ring trees are where Ringba runs the auction. Matthias Musters splits the setup into two layers. The ring tree target is a normal destination with hours, caps, and concurrency, plus a request URL your buyer supplies for pinging. The ring tree houses one or more of those targets. In the demo, the ring tree carries a minimum revenue of $29.01. If no dynamic bid clears that floor, the call drops to a static buyer paying $29, then to one paying $25 [WOqDYpchQOo @ 00:03:31]. Selling into RingbaX follows an exact recipe. Create RingbaX as a buyer, and name the ring tree target by category and traffic source. Toggle dynamic number so the destination arrives during the ping and post, and set Pacific time. Paste the seller offer's bid URL with appended parameters and use GET. Parse the bid with JPath on bidAmount and parse call acceptance with JavaScript. Then build a ring tree named with an RT suffix, with zero minimum revenue and zero failure revenue. It converts on dynamic call length from connect, with a 10-second dial timeout and a 3,000 ms ping timeout [uDzWrD17wqg @ 00:02:04]. On the buy side, RingbaX offers static or Ringba RTB destinations. A higher minimum duration lowers your priority in the exchange, and hitting the daily budget stops all bidding [wyW52qkPCrc @ 00:02:26].

ceohec runs the same machine on Retreaver, which they describe as free to open and pay-as-you-go at roughly 4 cents a minute. They enable performance marketing and RTB from the shopping cart, then split campaigns by vertical and even by buffer time. They quote auto insurance buffers at anywhere from 90 to 180 seconds. The route needs only dummy data, and the IVR prompts should be left alone [RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:01:09]. The default conversion criteria act as a fallback, such as a $40 lowest bid on a 120-second auto buffer, while the real bids live as tags at the publisher level. For a publisher such as Market Call, ceohec creates an RTB postback key with a TTL of 45 seconds and a 5-second timeout. They send the link over Telegram and tag the conversion criteria to the exact campaign ID, because without a response to the publisher's ping you get no calls [RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:08:03]. Buyers on RTB still need a dummy number plus a pass-through ping webhook. More negative priority wins first, and a buyer left out of the campaign receives nothing. TrackDrive's launch discipline closes the loop. Place real test calls end to end, then start with conservative caps and widen them as quality proves out [ncatAE6wf_0 @ 00:02:38].

callout.title: Small settings that protect the spread
callout.body: Four settings that keep billing clean, conversions in sync, supply private, and connect rates high.
items: Pitch publishers an extra 8 seconds on the buffer, so 120 seconds becomes 128. That way, connect and ring time never leave you paying for a call your buyer did not pay for [ceohec — RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:09:59]

Turn on conversion propagation when routing Retreaver to Retreaver. The 3 to 5 seconds it takes to connect on a 90-second buffer otherwise makes your conversions and the buyer's disagree [ceohec — RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:06:05]
Keep publisher names and IDs out of fields that buyer collaborators can see, because that is sensitive info you do not want to release [ceohec — RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:07:05]
Route to SIP whenever the buyer accepts it. Faster connections, better voice quality, and data passed in the SIP header all lift conversion rates [Ringba — BOFMLupLrSM @ 00:03:59]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Static versus ping-post is the first fork, and the camps split hard. ceohec tells newcomers that most of the time you don't run static unless you have one buyer that can take the volume; static just means no ping post, while RTB pings the system to see if an available buyer exists and then posts the call through, so no DID is needed [RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:04:42]. ceohec reserves static for offers that are fine with calls hitting a cell phone the buyer toggles with pause and play. Ringba's buyer-side RingbaX walkthrough offers both static and Ringba RTB destinations but highly recommends RTB for the most control over how calls get bought [wyW52qkPCrc @ 00:00:38]. Ringba's masterclass refuses the either-or: a call center paying a flat $10 on a 1:30 duration and a pay-per-call network paying $11 after two minutes sit on the same routing plan as programmatic bidders, and every buyer gets pinged before the routing decision [yat7hRHHsKY @ 00:05:10]. Matthias Musters builds the hybrid concretely with a ring tree of dynamic targets above static targets and a $29.01 minimum revenue floor; if no bid clears it, the call falls to a static buyer paying $29, then one paying $25 [WOqDYpchQOo @ 00:03:50].

How the winner gets picked is the second split. Ringba's masterclass argues the raw top bid is not automatically the winner: ping buyer three bids $12 on a 1:30 duration, yet ping buyer one at $8 on a one-minute duration carries a higher probability of conversion, so Ringba scores every buyer on estimated earnings per call from previous behavior before deciding where the call goes [yat7hRHHsKY @ 00:08:04]. TrackDrive lays the options out as a menu rather than a doctrine: priority, weight, highest bid, historical earnings per call, or ping post, where buyers answer in real time whether they want the call and what they will pay [9uZila67hss @ 00:02:34]. ExclusiveLiveCall pushes back on the reflex to dump everything on the $200 buyer over the $120 and $150 buyers, because that buyer may have limited capacity, you may hold contractual volume commitments, or certain publishers may carry different buyer relationships [Hnh5huLjUoE @ 00:04:56]. ceohec runs the blunt version inside Retreaver: priority is set so whoever is bidding more gets the calls before anybody else, with the more negative number earning the higher priority [RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:11:41]. Four operators, four answers: modeled EPC, a selectable menu, contract-aware rules, and plain bid-ranked priority.

The fiercest contrast is what the system does with the caller before and after the bid. ceohec tells beginners to ignore the IVR prompts completely and leave them exactly as they are, using a 'this is Farmers Insurance, please state your name' greeting as the example of what not to build [RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:03:25]. ExclusiveLiveCall treats caller data as the backbone of matching instead: the system asks for a five-digit zip code through an IVR, or a conversational AI receptionist asks what service the caller needs, hears 'my air conditioner stopped working,' tags it HVAC, and then collects the zip conversationally [Hnh5huLjUoE @ 00:03:10]. On dead calls, Ringba's answer is mechanical overflow: if ping buyer one doesn't answer, the call drops, or there's a busy signal, the platform reruns the process and routes to another ping buyer or a normal routing-plan buyer because it will not let that phone call die [yat7hRHHsKY @ 00:04:41]. ExclusiveLiveCall pushes past overflow into recovery: when a contractor is not answering at 8:00 at night, an AI receptionist schedules a slot on the buyer's calendar, turning a call worth $0 into a monetizable appointment, or banks the stated need and zip code as a lead record for a different monetization path [Hnh5huLjUoE @ 00:12:04].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive firsthand trap is billing duration drift. ceohec explains that connecting a call takes 3, 4, 5 seconds, so on a 90-second buffer you lose time to latency, and for Retreaver-to-Retreaver routing conversion propagation has to be switched on so the conversion on the buyer's end fires on your end too [RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:06:05]. The bigger fix is negotiated, not technical: when buying from a publisher like Market Call on a 120-second buffer at $30, ceohec asks for 8 extra seconds so the call converts at 128 seconds, because ringing time otherwise leaves you paying the publisher for a call your buyer never paid you for [RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:10:15]. RingbaX adds a buyer-side twist: minimum duration is only available on static routing, and the higher you set it, the less priority the campaign gets in the exchange [wyW52qkPCrc @ 00:02:26]. Ringba's masterclass shows why duration matters inside the auction itself, treating an $8 bid on a one-minute duration as a higher conversion probability than a $12 bid on 1:30 [yat7hRHHsKY @ 00:07:47]. ceohec's rule is flat: always add on that latency before the publisher deal is signed, or eat the gap between your buy-side and sell-side timers on every call.

Silent configuration errors kill volume before a single caller hears a ring. ceohec warns that when a publisher pings your system you need a response, and with no conversion criteria set up you won't get calls; the walkthrough then hits the trap live, forgetting that the conversion tag's campaign ID must match the auto insurance campaign ID 6DB and having to go back into the Market Call publisher to retag it [RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:09:15]. The same build flags that a call buyer added to a campaign is live right away, so the safe move is to click pause buyer until that buyer is ready and let them press play themselves through collaborator access [RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:15:37]. Ringba's account setup warns that skipping billing verification and the required document upload can disrupt service when the card cannot be billed [8ojiGzzsrV0 @ 00:00:19]. TrackDrive names test calls as the step most often skipped and the cheapest to do: place real calls start to finish, then check the call is tracked, routed to the right buyer, answered, timed correctly, and recorded as expected, so a mistake costs a few phone calls instead of a whole day of wasted traffic [ncatAE6wf_0 @ 00:02:38].

Unit economics break hardest on calls that look good and still go wrong. ceohec describes the area-code routing trap: a Texas-licensed buyer gets a 214 Dallas caller who has moved to Florida, where the buyer is not licensed, and you will most likely refund the buyer and still eat the call, a rare one-off but a real loss [RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:12:49]. ExclusiveLiveCall frames the no-answer loss: the publisher may already have paid Google $50 or $100 for the click, the consumer and the intent were real, and because nobody picked up, the opportunity disappears unless overflow or recovery catches it [Hnh5huLjUoE @ 00:10:01]. Recordings cut the other way too. One Ringba-titled upload is a parody of the onboarding pitch that ends in an investigator's exposé: a supposed travel company running campaigns named 'USA Blue Screen of Death' and 'UK adult' recorded every call through Ringba as its VoIP provider, and those recordings let outsiders listen in on fake tech-support pitches [RVobRCTpSEg @ 00:04:08]. A companion parody mocks the RTB pitch itself as a way to 'drop bids when lawsuits rise' [eLfL-CGZaa4 @ 00:01:21]. Every recorded call becomes a permanent trail of what the operation actually sells.

callout.title: Pre-Launch Kill Switches
callout.body: Four practitioner-reported pitfalls that must be cleared before paid traffic touches the routing plan.
items: Do not send paid traffic until real test calls confirm tracking, buyer routing, an answer, correct timing, and recording end to end [TrackDrive — ncatAE6wf_0 @ 00:02:38].
Do not accept a publisher's billable duration until it carries the 8-second latency pad over your buyer's buffer [ceohec — RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:09:59].
Do not add a call buyer to a campaign before they are ready; they go live immediately, so hit pause buyer first [ceohec — RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:15:37].
Do not launch a ring tree without a minimum revenue floor and static targets underneath it to catch bids that fall short [Ringba — WOqDYpchQOo @ 00:03:50].

chapters.pull_quote: "Before we allow a legitimate opportunity to die, we want the routing engine to look for additional ways to monetize it." — ExclusiveLiveCall (Hnh5huLjUoE @ 00:08:34).
action_checklist: Split campaigns by vertical and by buffer time, running a separate campaign for the same offer at a different duration [ceohec — RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:01:45].
Create each publisher's RTB postback key with TTL at 45 seconds and timeout at 5 seconds, then send the link to the publisher's rep [ceohec — RWVdTqjVYE8 @ 00:08:03].
Connect targets over SIP whenever the buyer accepts it for higher voice quality and faster connection times [Ringba — 8ojiGzzsrV0 @ 00:02:20].

Build the RingbaX seller ring tree with minimum and failure revenue at zero, convert on dynamic call length, dial timeout 10 seconds, and ping timeout 3,000 milliseconds [Ringba — uDzWrD17wqg @ 00:02:04].
Switch on duplicate call reporting and payout once per caller so one caller ID cannot trigger multiple publisher payouts [Ringba — BOFMLupLrSM @ 00:01:12].
Download call recordings from Ringba reporting and run them through AI transcription to mine neighborhoods and micro-services by zip code [Automate & Chill By Abhishek Sood — g7SAWXINXDo @ 00:03:13].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I build IVRs and call flows that pre-qualify callers before they reach a buyer?
chapters.title: IVR Design and Call Flows That Pre-Qualify Callers
chapters.subtitle: How IVR works, Ringba IVR, Dial IVR and call flows, profitable call-flow builds, quiz-funnel pre-qualification, visual flow builders (SignalWire, WildJar, RingCentral, Autocia), IVR best practices, Retell AI inbound webhooks, and GoHighLevel inbound routing
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from Ringba, Landerlab, SignalWire, WildJar, GetVoIP and independent operators agree on one rule: the IVR is a qualification gate that sorts callers on the attribute that decides payout before any buyer phone rings. Ringba's debt example forwards only callers with more than $10,000 in unsecured credit card debt. Carlos Corona's ACA flow routes uninsured callers into RTB and re-asks anyone who claims coverage, because many callers press the wrong key the first time. Corona does not monetize non-qualified Medicare and Medicaid callers as calls. He converts them into an IVR SMS opt-in, and the opt-in webhook carries the call UUID, the E.164 number, the campaign and the state. Landerlab pushes quiz answers such as carrier into Ringba URL parameters so router filters can use them. Practitioners disagree on two points. The first is whether to route mismatched callers to adjacent buyers, which Corona says breeds complaints. The second is whether to use audible menus or silent background IVR functions.

key_metrics.value: More than $10,000 in unsecured credit card debt (press 1 = qualified, press 2 = not qualified)
key_metrics.context: Jordan Soto's example of an IVR call flow where only the press-1 caller is forwarded to the buyer and the affiliate earns credit.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus: Qualify Before the Buyer Ever Rings
paragraphs: Every builder in this chapter treats the IVR as a qualification gate, not a greeting. Ringba defines interactive voice response as an automated system for qualifying callers with prompts and routing them to a destination based on their responses. It splits campaign routing into two modes. Standard routing sends calls to targets by priority and weight. IVR routing pushes callers into a node tree that hands off to a routing plan at the IVR level [Vd_ZoE2BRqQ @ 00:00:01] [Vd_ZoE2BRqQ @ 00:00:19]. Jordan Soto lays out the pay-per-call version plainly with a debt campaign. The caller is asked whether they carry more than ten thousand dollars in unsecured credit card debt. Pressing one means qualified, and the call is forwarded to the buyer. Pressing two means not qualified. Only the qualified leg earns the affiliate the commission [4dnXkZ7u6zw @ 00:00:51]. Carlos Corona runs the same logic on ACA traffic. A coverage question plays up front, and callers without Medicaid, Medicare, or employer coverage go straight into the RTB process against the buyers on that routing plan [tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:00:45]. The shared premise is that a buyer's phone should ring only after the caller has already sorted themselves on the one or two attributes that decide payout. Any call that reaches a buyer without that sort is a call the publisher is gambling on rather than selling.

Pre-qualification does not have to start at the keypad. Landerlab says anyone running pay-per-call to big auto insurance brands such as Allstate or Geico has to pre-qualify visitors before sending them to a buyer. Its build is a quiz funnel that asks for the visitor's current carrier and homeowner status. Those answers are then pushed into Ringba, where the call flow routes on them and filters exclusive buyers on homeowner or insured status [DMS29IlU8pE @ 00:00:01]. CallCentreHelper describes the silent side of an IVR. Some contact centers never want callers to hear a traditional menu at all. They still run background modules that connect into back-end systems and identify the caller from the number they display [8f7qA0z-AgQ @ 00:01:31]. Calilio and GetVoIP both stress the payoff of collecting context before the transfer. The agent who answers already knows what the caller needs instead of going in blind [KT-Jaz-hayQ @ 00:00:21] [U9IWvkKvtWE @ 00:01:08]. For an arbitrage operator the translation is direct. The qualifying data can come from a landing-page quiz, a keypad press, or a caller-ID lookup. Either way, it has to land on the call record before the routing decision is made. That is the only way to filter buyers on carrier, homeowner, or insured status instead of handing them whoever happens to dial in.

The builders also agree on construction order and flow hygiene. Ringba's training says that before you can create a call flow, you need a routing plan configured. The dial node at the end of the tree needs a destination to hand callers to [Ua5XxaPrhRs @ 00:01:05]. Ringba's IVR builder then refuses to save a tree missing a validation node. The error is outlined in red until a hang-up node catches calls that fail to connect to the routing plan [Vd_ZoE2BRqQ @ 00:02:22]. WildJar's James hits the same wall in his demo. Saving fails, and red lines appear around any transfer that has no target number configured. The flow stays broken until every branch has a place to dial [5z0mahGmR40 @ 00:01:53]. GetVoIP's Nate pushes menu discipline on top of that structure. His rules are to use a drag-and-drop builder, keep the phrasing concise, cap each menu at five options, and list the most common items first so most callers recognize their path immediately [7vsOEhARsdU @ 00:02:23]. Put together, the consensus template has four parts: a short qualifying question asked up front, a hard qualified branch to the buyer, a defined branch for non-qualified callers, and no dangling node anywhere. Every vendor demo, from Ringba to WildJar, blocks publishing on an open end. That block is the cheapest quality control an operator gets.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Carlos Corona's ACA flow is the most complete pay-per-call build in this chapter, and it runs on two keypad prompts. The opening message reads: We are one step closer to getting you approved for help with gas, groceries, and rent. Please press two if you do not have Medicare, Medicaid, or employer coverage. Please press one if you do have it. A press of two qualifies the caller and kicks off the RTB process to the buyers on the routing plan [tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:01:22]. A press of one does not end the call. Corona replays a longer version that opens with: please listen carefully as our menu has changed. The replay splits into one for Medicaid, two for Medicare, and three for no government health benefits, and a press of three routes back to the buyers [tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:01:55]. His reason comes straight from live traffic. A lot of people press something that was not the correct answer, and the second pass gives them another chance to make the right choice [tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:02:30]. SignalWire's Nicholas builds the same safety net generically. An attempt variable increments each time the gather times out or receives unknown input. A short audio cue plays before the caller loops back to the prompt. After two failed attempts, the flow disconnects the call [VByuomL6T0s @ 00:05:14].

Corona treats callers who confirm Medicaid or Medicare as no-value calls. Instead of hanging up on them, he converts them into an SMS opt-in. He builds a gather that accepts only a press of one. He lists the elements an IVR consent has to carry: the brand name, how to opt out, where to see the terms, and that message rates apply [tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:05:10]. His live script reads: Thank you for calling Medicare benefits. All agents are busy. Press one to complete your request via text. By pressing one, you agree to automated texts. To opt out, reply stop. Message rates apply. For terms, visit medicarebenefits.net/terms [tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:06:06]. A press of one fires a webhook with four fields: the inbound call UUID for reference if issues come up, the phone number in E.164 format for later texting, a campaign tag, and the state for time zones. The flow then dials a confirmation routing plan whose target only plays a message-sent prompt, and every dial records the entire call [tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:08:44]. Henryk Brzozowski's Retell AI setup shows the webhook limits operators must design around. The timeout is 10 seconds, with up to three retries before a silent fallback to the default agent. He also whitelists IPs so only Retell can reach his make.com endpoint [p7WavoW_6to @ 00:04:24].

Ringba's node set is the toolkit most of these pay-per-call builds run on. The dial node routes to a target, and the menu node decides on the key pressed. The router node decides on filters, and the gather node collects numerical input. The hours node routes on hours of operation, and the pixel node fires pixels from inside the call flow. The JS node runs custom JavaScript once the team activates it, and the profile node pulls enriched caller data [Ua5XxaPrhRs @ 00:03:42]. The robocall verification template asks every caller to press one to continue and automatically terminates anything that cannot, so spam robocallers never reach targets [Ua5XxaPrhRs @ 00:04:54]. On the buyer side, Shane Hitchcock explains Dial IVR. The operator times how long a buyer's own IVR takes to ask for a keypress and enters that timing. Ringba then sends the DTMF digit, or a dynamic tag such as a zip code, without the caller hearing it [VQKxVnPn5zE @ 00:01:15]. Landerlab's carrier routing connects the page to the flow in three steps. First, create a URL parameter named carrier, with carrier as the report name. Next, add a router whose filters read carrier equal to Allstate or Geico, with a routing plan behind each one. Finally, place a live test call and confirm the carrier tag shows up on the call log [DMS29IlU8pE @ 00:12:40].

callout.title: Small IVR tweaks the operators swear by
callout.body: These come from live builds and test calls, not from vendor feature lists.
items: Mix different voices across IVR prompts. Corona found that people pay more attention when the voice changes, while a single voice lets them tune out [Carlos Corona — tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:07:06].
Treat buyer IVRs as conversion killers. Use Dial IVR to send DTMF tones in the background so callers skip menus they never needed to hear [Ringba — VQKxVnPn5zE @ 00:00:15].
Preview the landing page and confirm the base number has been swapped. If the number is replaced, the Ringba number pool script is loading correctly [Landerlab — DMS29IlU8pE @ 00:10:33].
Dynamic variable names must match exactly between the webhook response and the agent prompt, or the caller's name will not populate [Henryk Brzozowski — p7WavoW_6to @ 00:07:13].

sop_steps.title: Stand up the routing plan first
sop_steps.action: Create the routing plan and choose priority routing or RPC routing before building any call flow.
sop_steps.detail: Priority routing sends calls by priority and weight. RPC routing sends calls by a target's revenue and historical performance. Then set how each target counts conversions, its revenue amount, and how duplicate conversions are handled [Ringba — Ua5XxaPrhRs @ 00:01:24].

sop_steps.title: Front-load the payout qualifier with a re-ask
sop_steps.action: Open the flow with a coverage or eligibility gather, send qualified presses to RTB, and replay a longer menu to callers who answer the other way.
sop_steps.detail: Corona's longer replay starts with please listen carefully as our menu has changed. It splits Medicaid, Medicare, and no coverage onto separate keys, so callers who pressed the wrong key get a second chance [Carlos Corona — tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:01:55].

sop_steps.title: Add an error loop and close every node
sop_steps.action: Increment an attempt variable on timeouts and unknown input, loop back once with an audio cue, and end in hang-up or voicemail.
sop_steps.detail: Nicholas disconnects after two failed attempts. He ties off the remaining error paths with stop recording, an apology played through TTS, a voicemail recording, and a hang-up [SignalWire — VByuomL6T0s @ 00:05:14].

sop_steps.title: Convert no-value callers into SMS opt-ins
sop_steps.action: Route non-qualified callers to a press-one consent gather, fire a webhook, and dial a recorded confirmation routing plan.
sop_steps.detail: The webhook passes the inbound call UUID, the E.164 phone number, the campaign tag, and the state. Every dial should record the entire call for later reference [Carlos Corona — tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:08:27].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether the caller should ever hear a qualifying menu. Carlos Corona builds the ACA flow around one: the inbound call plays a message asking whether the caller has Medicaid, Medicare, employer coverage or no insurance, and only the no-insurance press triggers the RTB hunt across the buyers under that routing plan [tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:00:30]. Ringba's own walkthrough of the three core flows frames the audible IVR the same way, using a debt example where callers with more than ten thousand dollars in unsecured credit card debt press one and everyone else presses two and falls out [4dnXkZ7u6zw @ 00:00:51]. Shane Hitchcock at Ringba argues the opposite side of the wire: IVRs can be conversion killers for any call campaign, so Ringba's Dial IVR uses software and DTMF tones to bypass a buyer's unnecessary menus without the customer ever hearing it, timing how long the prompt takes and injecting a press one or even a zip code tag [VQKxVnPn5zE @ 00:00:15]. CallCentreHelper adds that some contact centers refuse a traditional audible IVR entirely yet still run its silent functions, connecting to back-end systems and identifying the caller from the displayed telephone number [8f7qA0z-AgQ @ 00:01:31]. The operator choice is screening friction on your side versus raw speed into the buyer's live agent.

A second fork is where qualification data gets captured in the first place. Landerlab skips the keypad and qualifies on the landing page: a quiz asks the current insurance carrier and homeowner status, injects the Ringba number pool script, pushes the carrier value into a URL parameter, and a router node with filters sends Allstate and Geico callers to separate routing plans [DMS29IlU8pE @ 00:12:18]. Ringba's warm transfer model puts a human in that seat instead, where a qualifying call center agent asks a list of questions before handing off, and the conversion event typically lands on the transfer [4dnXkZ7u6zw @ 00:01:24]. Henryk Brzozowski routes before any agent speaks, using a Retell AI inbound webhook to make.com that checks the current time and the caller number, then returns a day agent armed with a transfer tool or a night agent stripped of it [p7WavoW_6to @ 00:01:31]. On the voice-versus-keypad question, Calilio pitches NLP systems that open with how can I help you today and route on full sentences rather than press one prompts, a direct challenge to the DTMF menus every pay-per-call builder here still relies on [KT-Jaz-hayQ @ 00:02:02]. Each choice moves the filter to a different layer of the stack, with different costs.

Practitioners also split hard on what to do with callers who fail the screen. Carlos Corona notes some publishers push Medicare callers to Medicare buyers, and strongly discourages it because the ad angle is ACA, the caller references that ad once on the phone with the agent, and the mismatch breeds complaints; the alternative playbook is an IVR SMS consent gather that names the brand, the opt-out, the terms page and message rates, then fires a webhook so the caller can be monetized by text with another offer [tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:03:55]. Routing logic splits too: Ringba offers priority routing by priority and weight, or RPC routing by a target's revenue and historical performance [Ua5XxaPrhRs @ 00:01:24]. For the call-back side, the GoHighLevel for Commercial Real Estate operator calls it personal preference with no right or wrong answer, weighing direct connect to a cell phone, which gives a real-time call back but zero prep time, against an IVR offering press one to book an appointment or press two for a call back [7GRJx9A5y5c @ 00:00:33]. GetVoIP pushes a different menu philosophy entirely: limit each menu to five options and let callers reach an agent at any time [7vsOEhARsdU @ 00:02:07]. Pick the policy that matches whether you sell every call or only the clean ones.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap Carlos Corona reports is trusting the first keypress. Testing showed a lot of callers press something that is not the correct answer, so a press one for coverage triggers a second, longer menu that opens with please listen carefully as our menu has changed and splits Medicaid, Medicare and no government benefits into separate keys before a call is written off [tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:02:13]. Corona also found callers tune out a single voice, and swapping voices across prompts keeps them alert, a finding credited to plain testing [tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:07:06]. Spam is the other leak: Ringba's robocall verification template plays a text-to-speech press one to continue, and any robocaller unable to complete it has the call automatically terminated before it ever reaches a target [Ua5XxaPrhRs @ 00:04:54]. SignalWire's Nicholas handles callers who time out or hit an unknown input with a set variables module that increments an attempt counter, plays an audio file confirming something went awry, loops back to the gather, and disconnects after two failed attempts [VByuomL6T0s @ 00:04:54]. Without that loop, confused callers either get dumped or route blind, and both outcomes burn paid traffic.

Build errors stall launches more often than strategy does. Ringba's IVR builder refuses to save a tree that lacks a hang-up node for calls that fail to connect to the routing plan, marking the error in red on the node [Vd_ZoE2BRqQ @ 00:02:22]. WildJar's James hit the same wall live: the save failed with red lines around both transfers because no target number had been configured for sales or support [5z0mahGmR40 @ 00:01:53]. Landerlab's call flow threw publish errors until each router branch had a routing plan selected, and the team verified the number pool script by checking that the base number on the page was replaced by a Ringba pool number before running a live mobile test and reading the carrier tag in the call log [DMS29IlU8pE @ 00:10:33]. Webhook routing carries its own failure state: Henryk Brzozowski found the Retell inbound webhook has a ten-second timeout, retries up to three times, and then defaults to the agent already set on the number, so a slow make.com scenario lands callers on that fallback agent; the dynamic variable name must also match exactly, and the webhook was locked down by whitelisting the Retell IP [p7WavoW_6to @ 00:04:24]. Test every branch end to end before buying traffic.

Economics leaks show up after the build, not during it. Autocia Technologies' Sanya warns that channels cap concurrent calls: five channels means five people can call together without anyone getting a busy tone, and the dashboard tracks answered, not answered and canceled calls plus answer rate per number [tdZ944Oycuo @ 00:02:28]. Missed calls need a recovery path, so WildJar routes unanswered transfers to voicemail with an instant missed-lead email and SMS alert to the sales team [5z0mahGmR40 @ 00:03:32]. The GoHighLevel for Commercial Real Estate operator sets the system to notify the agent whenever a caller hangs up without booking or requesting a call back, and calls direct connect a lost opportunity when the phone rings mid-tour or at a closing with zero prep time [7GRJx9A5y5c @ 00:03:15]. Carlos Corona's opt-in webhook passes the inbound call UUID, the E.164 phone number, the campaign tag and the state, so any issue can be traced back to how the caller opted in; the flow then dials a confirmation routing plan that plays a your message has been sent message, and every dial records the entire call [tf4AieS7Mhc @ 00:08:27]. Skip any of these and paid calls die unbilled or untraceable.

chapters.question_prompt: How do I route calls to the highest-converting buyer and attribute every call to its traffic source?
chapters.title: Routing Optimization and Call Attribution
chapters.subtitle: Automated precision routing, tag routing filters, URL parameters as tags, SIP routing, routing methods explained, dynamic number pool tracking, and call tracking tools compared (Invoca, CallRail, CallPOP, CloudTalk)
chapters.executive_summary: Pay-per-call operators teaching on Ringba's channel agree on one premise: whoever owns the call tracking and routing layer owns the margin. Adam of Ringba argues that affiliates running on network numbers lose control of busy-signal recovery, ring-timeout rerouting, duplicate remonetization and geo-accurate routing, and that duplicate routing alone typically pays for the platform, with duplicates running 5% to 25% of call flow. Jordan Soto and Mattias Mesters translate that into configuration: priority tiers, weight fractions, concurrency and dollar caps, hours of operation with lunch breaks, tag routing filters fed by URL parameters, and SIP delivery. Attribution vendors CallPOP, Invoca and Travis Wilkie's CallRail walkthrough split between static source numbers and dynamic number pools, while tool reviewers split on pricing: CallRail looks cheap until add-ons triple the bill, Invoca is quote-only enterprise, Ringba targets pay-per-call.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The baseline every Ringba speaker repeats is that a publisher who runs on a network's or broker's number has surrendered the call flow. Adam's masterclass puts it bluntly: without your own call tracking you cannot prioritize or weight buyers, and whoever handed you the number is the only party that ever receives the call [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:02:05]. Jordan Soto restates the same rule for rerouting, telling media buyers and publishers who rely on a network's tracking that they are simply out of luck when a buyer is busy or never answers [0QJvQjrUoX8 @ 00:00:57]. The pain compounds with scale. Adam describes clients moving from a handful of calls to 20 or 50 a day, then to thousands and tens of thousands daily, which is called completely normal in the space, and warns that operators lacking automated rerouting will get absolutely murdered by their buyers [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:08:53]. Soto frames duplicate handling the same way: networks typically refuse to pay for repeat callers, and only independent tracking lets the publisher keep control and get paid [ytuZI-5RwoI @ 00:00:39]. The shared prerequisite is an owned routing layer sitting between every tracking number and every destination, even for affiliates who still sell through networks.

Outside the pay-per-call bubble, attribution vendors land on the same foundation: a distinct number for every source you want to measure. CallPOP's walkthrough starts with buying local or toll-free numbers, assigning each one a source label and a receiving number, and notes that for publications, signs and billboards those two parameters are all you need before calls start flowing [wr6G-Sojm50 @ 00:01:13]. For web traffic the consensus shifts to dynamic pools. Invoca's website tag swaps static numbers for dynamic ones unique to each visitor, treating each number as a session identifier while capturing UTM source, medium, paid search keyword and Google click ID [bJeLdEIwej8 @ 00:00:35]. Jordan Soto describes Ringba's version as number swapping or DNI that locks a pool number to a browser session until the visitor goes idle, closes the browser or leaves, and tracks impressions whether or not the visitor ever calls [pNWCpdBjuPA @ 00:00:35]. Travis Wilkie, demonstrating CallRail, gives the street-level reason: without call tracking it is next to impossible to tell where calls come from, which is the old line about knowing half your marketing works but not which half [eH4764v8-74 @ 00:01:44]. Every speaker treats source-level numbers as table stakes before any routing decision means anything.

The third point of agreement is that the operator has to do their own quality assurance, because nobody else in the value chain will. Adam reports having hosted the CEO of almost every pay-per-call network on the Pay Per Caller show, and that 100% of them said to listen to call recordings, ideally playing them in the background to catch weak back-end buyers or duplicated IVR trees burning conversions [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:48:23]. Travis Wilkie lands in the same place from the local-business side, saying that replaying sales recordings exposes things you thought you were doing and were not, plus habits you never noticed [eH4764v8-74 @ 00:04:40]. Invoca's brand testimonial quantifies what conversation data unlocked once calls were tied to revenue instead of clicks and impressions: a 33 percent efficiency gain that let the team cut wasted ad spend, and 45% of people likely to hit voicemail now scheduling appointments online [IPh2uXrQS1A @ 00:00:57]. The consensus extends to buyer caps. Adam insists new buyers capping you at ten calls a day while you push 300 is fair, because a human must answer and vet each call, and once your quality is proven those same caps keep competitors out of the campaign [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:34:44]. Pay-per-call, in that telling, is exclusionary rather than inclusive.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Mattias Mesters walks through the core routing plan math in Ringba: priority one targets are always tried first, priority two only when none of them is available, and within a tier the weights become fractions, so targets weighted 1, 6, 6 and 1 split traffic 1/14, 6/14, 6/14 and 1/14 [0eCCbtHmCJE @ 00:02:34]. Error handling sits on top. Adam describes Ringba detecting a busy signal within a few milliseconds and immediately dialing buyer two, fast enough that no caller can notice, which neutralizes call centers that oversell capacity to many publishers and then busy-signal overflow so they never pay for it [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:05:07]. For buyers who let calls ring 30 seconds instead of bouncing them, the fix is a ring timeout configured at the buyer or target level, maybe five seconds, maybe ten, after which the call is pulled and rerouted [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:08:15]. Adam pairs that with a commercial term: if a ringing buyer imposes duration requirements, bill on duration from the moment the call starts ringing rather than from answer, because the buyer captured the option value of picking up the whole time [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:06:38]. Adam actually prefers busy-signal buyers, since the bounce arrives in real time.

Simultaneous dialing rings every eligible buyer at once, whether three or 600, and the first to answer wins the call, but Adam flags the trap: if buyer one pays $10, buyer two $22 and buyer three $6, and buyer three always answers fastest, sim-dial gets expensive, and mixed West Coast and East Coast requirements break it too [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:11:41]. The ideal setup is nationwide buyers paying roughly the same, such as $10, $10 and $10.25, on raw calls with no duration requirement [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:12:36]. Concurrency is the next lever. Adam recommends configuring buyer concurrency hourly by day rather than flat, after asking each call center when lunch costs them 20% of capacity, when the 2 p.m. shift change adds seats and when half the agents leave at 7 p.m., and on big direct campaigns having someone talk to buyer operations daily [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:57:17]. Caps protect cash as well as capacity. Jordan Soto suggests capping a new buyer at $2,000 for the first two weeks so they pay before more calls flow, and stopping delivery once a daily, weekly or monthly cap is hit because overage calls go unpaid [yFkULiyenzk @ 00:01:44].

The data layer is what turns routing into a margin weapon. Mattias Mesters shows Ringba tag routing filters on each target: any stored tag, whether passed by publishers, captured from a landing page via number pools or appended through instant caller profiles, can gate eligibility using logic such as begins with, contains, equals multiple values, exists, less than or greater than, with bulk zip lists and AND/OR rules, for example Alabama, Alaska, Arizona and Connecticut or listed zips, and only from test publisher one [4MDNmxviCKk @ 00:02:20]. URL parameters feed the same filters: declare the parameter under Integrations, keep the third party's name such as SRC or rename it to source, then select it in the target's filter dropdown [qr3oqapZvoo @ 00:01:08]. On the voice side, Jordan Soto says Ringba can auto-dial the selections inside a buyer's IVR so the caller never hears a second identical menu, lifting conversion [ETvzBEnleCs @ 00:02:03], and recommends SIP delivery to buyers who support it for faster connects, better audio and data passed in the SIP header [0QJvQjrUoX8 @ 00:00:19]. Together these filters replace the area-code guesswork Ringba's speakers blame for misrouting the roughly 35% of callers whose area code does not match their location.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Ringba's masterclass host, Adam, refuses to treat simultaneous dialing as a default. Sim-dial rings every eligible buyer at once, whether that is three, twenty-five or six hundred, and the first one to pick up owns the call, which maximizes answer rates [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:09:28]. The same session flags the trap immediately: if buyer one pays $10, buyer two pays $22 and buyer three pays $6, and buyer three always answers fastest, sim-dial turns into a very expensive situation, and split geographic requirements such as West Coast versus East Coast buyers break it outright [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:11:41]. The verdict is narrow: run sim-dial only when every buyer takes national traffic, payouts sit essentially level ($10, $10, $10.25), and buyers pay on raw call with no duration requirement, because then salesperson quality is irrelevant and speed to answer is the whole game [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:12:55]. Everywhere else, Mattias Mesters demonstrates the alternative playbook inside the routing plan: priority tiers where priority one is always tried first and priority two only when none of those targets are available, with weights acting as fractions, so four targets weighted 1, 6, 6 and 1 split traffic in fourteenths [0eCCbtHmCJE @ 00:02:15]. Waterfall control beats raw speed whenever payouts or eligibility diverge.

Duplicate callers split operators into two camps. The aggressive camp resells every repeat: Adam reports duplicate rates of at least 5% on the low end and up to 25% on the high end across hundreds of verticals, while networks refuse to pay for a duplicate roughly 98% of the time or more, so monetizing any slice of that band is pure profit [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:14:05]. Jordan Soto frames resale as stripping the network's margin: networks sell duplicates to multiple parties on the back end yet pay the publisher only once per caller, and your own tracking takes that margin away without them having any idea [0QJvQjrUoX8 @ 00:02:33]. The conservative camp pins repeats instead. On campaigns where consumers keep dialing back believing the number is customer service, Ringba lets you force a repeat caller to the same buyer over and over, and Adam stresses that the ability to resell never obligates you to [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:19:26]. The identical tension runs through buyer mix. Adam wants a deliberate blend of direct buyers, aggregators, brokers and networks: networks usually take a pretty high margin, yet a call answered at a loss through a network still beats letting it die unanswered [ojcbZuG798w @ 01:00:30]. Resell or pin, direct or network, the deciding variable is campaign type.

Attribution itself has rival playbooks. For geo-licensed verticals, Adam's primary route is number pool JavaScript that reads the caller's physical zip code, but the fallback when that is unavailable is brute structure: subdivide ad campaigns by state, from Michigan to Texas to California to every other state, then pass the region in the URL to the landing page or run 50 different tracking numbers, and tell buyers you only send callers physically in, say, Wisconsin regardless of area code [ojcbZuG798w @ 00:27:23]. On number assignment, Jordan Soto describes Ringba pools locking a number to one browser session until the visitor goes idle, closes the browser or leaves the page [pNWCpdBjuPA @ 00:00:35]. Invoca argues for recycling instead: set an attribution window matching buying behavior, so if customers typically call within 30 minutes, the uncalled number goes to a new visitor after 30 minutes, which makes one-to-one tracking feasible and keeps costs down [bJeLdEIwej8 @ 00:02:43]. CallPOP runs the leanest version for offline media, assigning one unique tracking number per marketing source or lead acquisition channel, pointed at a single receiving number for publications, signs and billboards [wr6G-Sojm50 @ 00:00:20]. Session-lock buys per-visitor certainty; Invoca's window reuse explicitly buys lower cost.
